common_name: Veitch's Peony (Dwarf Wild Chinese Species Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall with eyes 1-2 in below the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained soil; this compact wild species from high alpine meadows and scrub of western China forms a low, dome-shaped clump rather than the taller habit of garden hybrid peonies.

directions: Veitch's peony is a compact wild herbaceous species native to high alpine meadows and open scrub in Gansu, Sichuan, Shaanxi, and Qinghai provinces of China, named for the Veitch nursery dynasty that helped introduce it to Western gardens. It produces nodding, bowl-shaped flowers in shades of magenta-pink to pale pink or white, each centered with a cluster of bright yellow stamens, opening in late spring above finely cut, blue-green foliage. Unlike many garden hybrid peonies it spreads slowly by creeping rootstock into a broader clump over years rather than staying as a single crown. Leave it undisturbed once established, since like all peonies it resents root disturbance and may sulk for a season or two after transplanting.

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall with eyes 1-2 in below the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained soil in a lightly shaded woodland-edge setting; this far-northern wild species tolerates cold exceptionally well, reflecting its native range across Siberia and Central Asia.

directions: Siberian peony is a cold-hardy wild herbaceous species first described by Linnaeus from material collected near the Ural Mountains, with a natural range extending east across Siberia into northern China and Mongolia. Each stem typically carries a single outward-facing, saucer-shaped flower in magenta-red, occasionally fading to pink or white, with a prominent central tuft of golden stamens, opening in early summer above deeply divided, almost fern-like foliage. It naturally occurs in open woodland and scrub rather than meadow, so it tolerates and often prefers a lightly shaded site that mimics those conditions. Once settled it is extremely long-lived and needs little attention beyond an annual mulch and division only when clumps become congested.

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall with eyes 1-2 in below the soil surface in humus-rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil; this species comes from the western Himalaya and benefits from a cool root zone and some shelter from the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: Himalayan peony takes its name from the Latin term for its native range, emodi montes, the western Himalaya from Afghanistan through Kashmir to Nepal, where it grows in forest clearings and scrub at moderate elevation. It is among the taller wild peony species, sending up clumping stems that each carry several semi-pendent, cup-shaped, pure white flowers with a bold central boss of golden-yellow stamens in late spring. Its clean white color and relatively large flower size have made it a parent species behind some modern white-flowered peony hybrids. Site it where afternoon shade tempers the heat of the day, since it comes from cooler mountain forest margins and resents prolonged summer drought.

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall with eyes 1-2 in below the soil surface in gritty, sharply drained soil in a warm, sunny site; this Iberian native is adapted to dry rocky scrub and resents heavy, waterlogged soils.

directions: Iberian peony is a wild species endemic to rocky scrub and open woodland of Spain and Portugal, flowering unusually early in the peony world, often as soon as March or April in its native hills. It forms a low clump of glossy, dark green divided foliage topped by deep magenta to rose-pink cupped flowers with a central crown of yellow stamens. Its early bloom and compact stature make it well suited to a sunny rock garden or Mediterranean-style border rather than a traditional perennial bed. Give it sharp drainage and avoid summer irrigation once established, since in its native habitat it goes through the hottest months baked dry.

planting.note: Plant divisions or young container stock in fall in gritty, sharply drained soil in a sheltered, sunny site; in colder parts of its hardiness range it is often grown in a large pot that can be moved under cover for winter, since it is less cold-tolerant than most other wild peony species.

directions: Majorcan peony is endemic to limestone cliffs and scrub of the Balearic Islands, instantly recognizable by its red-tinted stems and leaves that are deep purple-red on the underside, a striking contrast to the deep rose-pink, strongly fragrant flowers that open in earliest spring. It is one of the least cold-hardy wild peony species, reflecting its mild island origin, and is grown by collectors through specialty rock-garden and Mediterranean seed exchanges rather than found in general nursery trade. Seedlings are slow, often taking several years to reach flowering size, so patience is rewarded rather than disappointed. Protect the crown from hard freezes and avoid summer waterlogging, since it is adapted to a dry, mild maritime climate.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this wild deciduous species from eastern China flowers very early on bare branches, so site it away from a frost pocket that could damage the display.

directions: Tianmu magnolia is a wild deciduous tree species discovered in the 1930s and native to a small area of Zhejiang, Jiangsu, and Anhui provinces in eastern China, closely related to the better-known Magnolia denudata and Magnolia stellata. It opens cup-shaped, lightly fragrant flowers in pale pink with a darker pink flush toward the base and a contrasting central cluster of purplish-red stamens, blooming on naked branches in early spring ahead of the foliage. Because it flowers so early, a sheltered site away from the coldest frost pockets helps protect the display from a late cold snap. It grows into a narrow, upright small tree over time and is mainly found through specialty magnolia nurseries and botanical garden plant sales rather than general retail.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online — International Dendrology Society

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this short-lived wild annual self-sows readily, so established plantings often return on their own in subsequent years.

directions: Flower-of-an-hour is a wild annual hibiscus native to the Old World and now widely naturalized across temperate North America, named for its fleeting cream to pale-yellow blooms marked with a deep maroon-purple throat that open fresh each morning and wilt by early afternoon. New flowers appear daily over a long summer season, followed by distinctive papery, inflated, lantern-like seed capsules formed from the enlarged calyx that persist and add interest after bloom. It thrives on neglect in lean, dry soil and is easily grown from direct-sown seed, making it a good choice for a wild-garden border, meadow planting, or anywhere a true species hibiscus with old-fashioned charm is wanted. Deadheading will not extend bloom but removing spent capsules can curb self-seeding if a tidier look is preferred.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service PLANTS Database

planting.note: Sow seed or plant container stock in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in full sun; this wetland species tolerates periodic flooding and is well suited to a pond margin, bog garden, or low-lying wet spot in frost-free climates.

directions: Swamp hibiscus is a wild perennial subshrub native to wetland margins across Africa, South and Southeast Asia, Australia, and Pacific islands, distinguished from its showier relatives by prickly stems and clear pale-yellow flowers with a dark maroon to red central eye, blooming from summer into fall. It is naturally found growing in and around marshes, ditches, and seasonally flooded ground, so it tolerates soggy soil and brief inundation far better than most other hibiscus species, while still appreciating full sun for best flowering. Where winters stay reliably frost-free it behaves as a long-lived perennial, dying back to the base after cooler weather and resprouting from the roots in spring. Outside its hardy range it is usually grown as a seasonal wetland-edge annual or overwintered in a greenhouse.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online
